questions.prompt: What lets a standard SRAM cell retain a bit while its word line is inactive?

options.text: Charge on an isolated capacitor is periodically refreshed
options.explanation: That describes the storage mechanism of conventional DRAM.

options.text: A single NAND gate stores the most recent input
options.explanation: A combinational gate alone has no state-holding feedback.

options.text: Two cross-coupled inverters reinforce a stable state while access transistors isolate it from the bit lines
options.explanation: Correct. Powered feedback maintains the bit; the word line controls access for reading or writing.

options.text: A clock repeatedly copies the bit into a flip-flop
options.explanation: The standard SRAM cell maintains its state through continuous feedback, without periodic clocked copying.

questions.workedExample: With the word line inactive, the access transistors disconnect the storage nodes from the bit lines. The two inverters continue to drive each other into one of two stable states. That powered feedback preserves the bit without refresh; removing power loses it.

questions.prompt: Why can a large SRAM cache consume substantial chip area even though one cell stores only one bit?

options.text: Each cache byte requires only one transistor
options.explanation: A byte contains multiple bits and each standard 6T cell uses multiple transistors.

options.text: All cache area is in the output wires
options.explanation: Storage cells, tags, protection and peripheral circuits all contribute.

options.text: Every data bit needs its own storage cell, with additional overhead beyond the data cells
options.explanation: Correct. Repeating a small multi-transistor cell many times adds up.

options.text: SRAM stores values without physical circuitry
options.explanation: The logical bit is maintained by powered transistor feedback.

questions.workedExample: Start with the physical storage unit: one 6T cell per data bit. More capacity repeats those cells and also requires access circuitry; tags and optional error protection add storage too. SRAM earns this area cost through its latency and integration advantages.

lessons.title: DRAM charge, row buffers and refresh
lessons.summary: DRAM activation senses and restores a row of capacitor-stored bits.
lessons.body:
## DRAM: one transistor and a capacitor

A dynamic RAM cell stores a bit as **charge on a tiny capacitor**, behind one access transistor:

```
 WL --------+
            | gate
 BL ------[ T ]------+
                     |
                   ===== C
                     |
                    plate
```

That is the **1T1C** cell, far smaller than 6T SRAM, which is why DRAM is the cheap, dense memory used for main memory.

The price is paid in behaviour:

- **Reads are destructive.** Raising WL connects the capacitor to a bit line with much larger capacitance. The charge spreads out ("charge sharing"), nudging the bit line voltage up or down by a small amount. The sense amplifier detects and amplifies this, and in doing so **writes the value back** into the cells of the row.
- **Rows, not words.** Activating a word line reads an entire row into the sense amplifiers, which act as a **DRAM row buffer**. Further reads from the same open row are much faster than opening a new one. This is why access patterns matter so much for DRAM performance (module 5).
- **Charge leaks.** Stored charge degrades, so the memory must periodically sense and restore its rows even when software makes no accesses. Refresh windows, commands and scheduling limits depend on the device, temperature and selected mode. Shortening the allowed refresh window while retaining the same command count requires more frequent refreshes.

Controllers must obey the selected part's timing and scheduling limits; affected banks cannot serve ordinary accesses during their refresh operation. A generic interval is not a controller specification.

- **A different process.** Making capacitors that hold enough charge in a tiny area needs special manufacturing, so commodity main-memory DRAM is commonly on separate dies, adding interface and interconnect costs. Embedded DRAM and integrated/stacked arrangements also exist; off-chip placement is not part of the definition of DRAM.

| | SRAM | DRAM |
|---|---|---|
| Cell | 6 transistors | 1 transistor + capacitor |
| Retention | while powered | ms; needs refresh |
| Read | non-destructive | destructive, rewritten |
| Typical use | registers, caches | main memory |
| Latency | depends on array and interface; usually favoured for low latency | depends on device, row state and interface |
| Cost per bit | high | low |

> [!example] Rowhammer
> DRAM cells are now so small and close together that repeatedly activating one row can disturb the charge in neighbouring rows. In 2014, researchers showed that hammering a row hundreds of thousands of times between refreshes could flip bits next door, and later work turned this into privilege-escalation exploits. Targeted refresh and error-correcting schemes can reduce risk, but neither generic TRR nor unspecified ECC guarantees immunity; effectiveness depends on the exact memory/controller and threat model. It is a reminder that the abstraction "memory holds bits" rests on analogue physics.

## Key takeaways
- DRAM activation senses and restores a row of capacitor-stored bits.
- Refresh requirements and disturbance mitigations depend on the device and operating conditions.

questions.prompt: Why must DRAM be refreshed, while SRAM does not need refreshing?

options.text: DRAM stores each bit as charge on a capacitor, which leaks away; SRAM's inverter loop actively holds its value
options.explanation: Correct. A DRAM cell is passive, so its charge decays over milliseconds and must be read and rewritten. SRAM's feedback loop restores itself continuously from the power supply.

options.text: DRAM is slower, so it needs extra cycles to catch up
options.explanation: Refresh has nothing to do with speed; it exists because the stored charge decays.

options.text: DRAM loses its contents every time the CPU writes to a different row
options.explanation: Writes to one row do not erase others. Refresh is needed even if the CPU never touches the memory at all.

options.text: SRAM is non-volatile, so it keeps data without power
options.explanation: SRAM is volatile: it loses its data when power is removed. It just doesn't need refreshing while powered.

questions.workedExample:
1. DRAM cell: one transistor plus a capacitor. The bit is the presence or absence of charge.
2. Real capacitors and transistors leak, so the charge decays. After long enough, a 1 is indistinguishable from a 0.
3. Refresh reads each row into the sense amplifiers, which restore full voltage and write it back. The permitted window depends on the selected device, temperature and refresh mode; use its datasheet.
4. SRAM cell: two cross-coupled inverters, each driving the other from the supply rails, so the stored value is continuously regenerated.

Both are volatile: cut the power and both forget.

questions.prompt: Which statements about SRAM and DRAM are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reading a DRAM cell disturbs its charge, so the sense amplifiers must write the row back
options.explanation: True. Charge sharing with the bit line destroys the stored level; activation senses and restores the row; subsequent column reads from the open row use the row buffer.

options.text: SRAM is used for CPU caches mainly because it is denser than DRAM
options.explanation: False. SRAM is much less dense (6 transistors per bit versus 1T1C). Caches use it because it is fast and built in the same CMOS process as the logic.

options.text: After a DRAM row has been opened, a read can avoid activation/precharge overhead compared with accessing a conflicting row in the same bank
options.explanation: True. The whole row sits in the sense amplifiers (the row buffer), so a hit in the open row skips the slow activation step.

options.text: Both SRAM and DRAM lose their contents when power is removed
options.explanation: True. Both are volatile. Non-volatile storage, such as flash, traps charge in a way that survives power-off.

options.text: SRAM needs a refresh cycle about every 64 ms, like DRAM
options.explanation: False. SRAM's cross-coupled inverters actively hold their value, so it never needs refresh. Only DRAM's leaking capacitors do.

questions.workedExample:
Compare the two cells:

```
          SRAM          DRAM
cell      6T loop       1T + cap
refresh   not required  device-specific
read      non-destr.    destructive
density   low           high
volatile  yes           yes
```

1. DRAM reads are destructive and rewritten (A true).
2. Caches use SRAM for speed and process compatibility, despite its low density (B false).
3. Open-row hits avoid re-activation (C true).
4. Both are volatile (D true).
5. Refresh is a DRAM-only cost (E false).

questions.prompt: A DRAM device's selected operating mode requires the same refresh-command count in a shorter permitted window. What must the controller do?

options.text: Refresh only when software reads the memory
options.explanation: Charge can decay even without software access.

options.text: Schedule refreshes more frequently while meeting the part's timing rules
options.explanation: Correct. The same required work must now finish in less time.

options.text: Leave the schedule unchanged because the bit capacity is unchanged
options.explanation: Capacity alone does not determine retention requirements.

options.text: Disable sense amplification to preserve the original charge
options.explanation: Sensing and restoration are how the stored values are maintained.

questions.workedExample: Refresh is a retention obligation imposed by the device and operating mode. Shortening the window tightens the scheduling requirement. The controller must accommodate the increased refresh demand and its access restrictions rather than assuming a universal interval.

lessons.title: Describe combinational and clocked hardware
lessons.summary: Concurrent HDL blocks describe hardware that operates in parallel.
lessons.body:
## Describing hardware: Verilog

Large digital designs are commonly described using RTL, alongside generated blocks and custom-designed circuit macros. Engineers write **register-transfer level (RTL)** descriptions in a hardware description language (HDL), mainly **Verilog**/**SystemVerilog** or **VHDL**, and a **synthesis** tool turns them into a netlist of gates and flip-flops from a cell library (or LUTs on an FPGA).

The crucial mental shift: Verilog looks like a programming language, but it describes **hardware that all exists and runs at once**, not one CPU executing the whole file sequentially. Procedural statements within a block still follow simulation scheduling and statement order.

### Combinational logic

The full adder from adder lessons:

```verilog
module full_adder(
  input  a, b, cin,
  output s, cout
);
  // The sum keeps odd parity of three bits.
  assign s    = a ^ b ^ cin;
  // Generate or propagate the carry.
  assign cout = (a & b) | (cin & (a ^ b));
endmodule
```

An `assign` is a permanent connection: whenever an input changes, the output follows, just like a gate. The two `assign` lines are two pieces of hardware side by side; their order is irrelevant.

In real designs you would just write `assign {cout, s} = a + b + cin;` and let the synthesis tool choose an adder structure (ripple, prefix and so on) that meets the timing target.

### Sequential logic

A 4-bit register with synchronous reset and a load enable:

```verilog
module reg4(
  input            clk, rst, load,
  input      [3:0] d,
  output reg [3:0] q
);
  // Reset wins over load at the same edge.
  always @(posedge clk)
    if (rst)       q <= 4'b0000;
    else if (load) q <= d;
endmodule
```

- `always @(posedge clk)` means "at each rising edge", so `q` becomes four D flip-flops.
- When neither condition holds, `q` keeps its value. Synthesis implements that with the mux in front of each D input, exactly as in sequential-logic lessons.
- `4'b0000` is a literal: 4 bits wide, binary.

## Key takeaways
- Concurrent HDL blocks describe hardware that operates in parallel.
- Continuous assignments model combinational functions; clocked non-blocking updates model registers.

questions.prompt: Following the standard clocked-RTL convention, which Verilog form should you use for a register that updates on the rising clock edge?

options.text: `assign q = d;`
options.explanation: `assign` describes a permanent combinational connection: q would follow d at all times, like a wire, with no memory.

options.text: `always @(*) q = d;`
options.explanation: `always @(*)` describes combinational logic, re-evaluated whenever an input changes. It does not wait for a clock edge.

options.text: `always @(posedge clk) q = d;` with a blocking assignment
options.explanation: This can infer a single register, but using blocking assignments for interacting clocked registers can make the result depend on statement order or introduce races. The conventional style uses non-blocking assignments for stored state.

options.text: `always @(posedge clk) q <= d;` with a non-blocking assignment
options.explanation: Correct. The edge event controls when the register samples; the non-blocking assignment schedules the update later, allowing race-free same-edge registers to read the old state.

questions.workedExample:
1. A register must change only at the clock edge, so the sensitivity list is `@(posedge clk)`.
2. Flip-flops all sample their inputs at the same instant. Non-blocking `<=` models that: each right-hand side is evaluated when its statement runs, and the stored-value updates occur in the later non-blocking-assignment region. In race-free same-edge RTL this preserves old-value sampling.
3. So: `always @(posedge clk) q <= d;`

Rule of thumb: `<=` in clocked blocks, `=` in `always @(*)` blocks, `assign` for simple combinational wires.

lessons.title: Verilog FSMs, scheduling and synthesis
lessons.summary: Non-blocking assignments preserve old-value sampling in the race-free example.
lessons.body:
### The FSM from sequential-logic lessons

The "two 1s in a row" Moore machine, written the standard way with one block for the state register and one for the next-state logic:

```verilog
module two_ones(
  input  clk, rst, x,
  output z
);
  localparam S0 = 2'b00, S1 = 2'b01,
             S2 = 2'b10;
  reg [1:0] state, next;

  // Capture state at each rising edge.
  always @(posedge clk)
    if (rst) state <= S0;
    else     state <= next;

  // Assign every branch: no storage here.
  always @(*)
    case (state)
      S0:      next = x ? S1 : S0;
      S1:      next = x ? S2 : S0;
      S2:      next = x ? S2 : S0;
      default: next = S0;
    endcase

  // Moore output uses only stored state.
  assign z = (state == S2);
endmodule
```

Compare it with the block diagram of an FSM: the first `always` block is the state register, the second is the next-state logic, and the `assign` is the Moore output logic. The `default` branch sends the unused code `11` back to S0, in the RTL simulation. This is not a general physical fault-recovery guarantee: synthesis may optimize unreachable encodings or re-encode the FSM. Use the tool's safe-state options and verify the synthesized implementation if illegal-state recovery is required. The synthesis tool derives the gate equations (and may re-encode the states, for example as one-hot).

### Blocking vs non-blocking assignment

Verilog has two assignment operators, and mixing them up is the most common beginner bug:

- `<=` (**non-blocking assignment**): a right-hand side is evaluated when its statement executes and the update is scheduled for the non-blocking-assignment region. In this race-free same-edge example, both right-hand sides read the old values. This models flip-flops, which all sample on the same edge. Use it in `always @(posedge clk)` blocks.
- `=` (**blocking**): updates immediately, so later lines see the new value. Use it in combinational `always @(*)` blocks.

```verilog
always @(posedge clk) begin
  a <= b;   // both read the old values:
  b <= a;   // a and b swap every cycle
end
```

With `=` instead, `a = b;` would happen first and `b = a;` would then copy the *new* `a`, so both end up holding the old `b`. In hardware terms you described a different circuit from the one you meant.

### Pitfalls

- **Accidental latches.** In intended combinational `always @(*)` logic, assign each output on every path. For independent input signals, `if (en) y = d;` with no `else` retains `y` when enable is low and normally infers a transparent latch. Synthesis may remove unreachable paths or unused storage, so inspect its reports. Supply an `else` or a suitable default to describe combinational behaviour.
- **Simulation-only code.** Simulation delays such as #5 do not specify physical gate delay in ordinary RTL synthesis. Some FPGA flows do synthesize supported initial blocks into power-up register or memory initialization; other constructs and ASIC flows differ. Check the target tool's supported subset.
- **Thinking in software.** A synthesizable fixed-bound loop may be unrolled, but data dependencies can make a combinational chain and optimizations can share or remove logic. A 1,000-iteration source loop does not guarantee exactly 1,000 physical copies. Explicit state/control is needed to spread work across clock cycles.

### From RTL to silicon

The flow after writing RTL is roughly:

1. **Simulate** with a testbench to check behaviour.
2. **Synthesise** into a gate-level netlist (lessons 2 and 3 done automatically, with multi-level optimisation).
3. **Place and route**: position every cell and draw every wire.
4. **Static timing analysis**: check setup and hold on every path (sequential-logic lessons), inserting buffers to fix hold violations.
5. For an FPGA, the result is a bitstream that configures LUTs and routing; for an ASIC, it is masks for fabrication.

## Key takeaways
- Non-blocking assignments preserve old-value sampling in the race-free example.
- Complete combinational assignments avoid unintended latches; synthesis and physical checks follow simulation.

## Further reading

options.text: a holds two and b holds one: they swap
options.explanation: That is what the non-blocking assignment version (`<=`) does. With blocking `=`, the second line sees the already-updated `a`.
This would happen if the lines ran in reverse order (`b = a` first). They run top to bottom, so `a` is updated first.
Correct. `a = b` sets a to 2 immediately; `b = a` then copies the new a, so b stays 2. Both end up holding the old b.

options.text: a holds one and b holds two: no change until the next edge
options.explanation: Assignments in a clocked block take effect at this edge. The only question is whether later lines see earlier updates.

questions.workedExample:
Blocking `=` updates immediately, like a software variable:

```
start:     a = 1, b = 2
a = b;  -> a = 2
b = a;  -> b = 2  (reads new a)
```

In this race-free swap fragment, each non-blocking `<=` evaluates its right-hand side when the statement runs; both updates occur in the later non-blocking-assignment region:

```
RHS: b = 2, a = 1
then: a <= 2, b <= 1   (swap)
```

Real flip-flops behave like `<=`: each samples its input from before the edge. That is why clocked blocks use `<=`.

options.text: A 3-to-1 mux, with `y` = 0 when sel = 11
options.explanation: Verilog does not default an unassigned output to 0. If no branch assigns `y`, it must keep its previous value.

options.text: A 4-to-1 mux with the fourth input left floating
options.explanation: Synthesis does not leave inputs floating. To keep `y` unchanged for sel = 11 it needs storage.

options.text: A mux plus a transparent latch, because `y` must remember its old value when sel = 11
options.explanation: Correct. With no assignment on that path, the code describes memory, and in a combinational block that means an inferred latch, with the timing problems latches bring.

options.text: A D flip-flop clocked by `sel`
options.explanation: Nothing in the code refers to a clock edge, so no flip-flop is inferred. The storage is level-sensitive: a latch.

questions.workedExample:
1. In `always @(*)`, the block describes what `y` is for every input combination.
2. List the paths: sel = 00, 01, 10 assign `y`. sel = 11 does not.
3. Verilog semantics: an unassigned variable keeps its old value. Hardware that keeps an old value is memory.
4. Synthesis therefore infers a latch enabled when sel ≠ 11. Tools usually warn ("inferred latch for y"), and the warning is easy to miss.

Fix by covering every path:

```verilog
else y = 1'b0;   // or
// defined default for valid inputs
```

questions.prompt: Look at the `two_ones` FSM module from the lesson (a clocked block for `state`, an `always @(*)` case statement for `next`, and `assign z = (state == S2)`). Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The two `always` blocks and the `assign` describe hardware that operates simultaneously, not code run in order
options.explanation: True. Each describes a separate piece of hardware, all active at once. Their order in the file does not matter.

options.text: `next` becomes a register, because it is declared with `reg`
options.explanation: False. `reg` is just a Verilog variable type. `next` is assigned in an `always @(*)` block on every path, so it synthesises to combinational logic. Only `state`, assigned on `posedge clk`, becomes flip-flops.

options.text: Without the default branch, RTL simulation at state 11 leaves next unassigned, creating unintended retention semantics
options.explanation: True for RTL simulation: next retains its previous value on that path. Generic synthesis can infer a latch, but FSM extraction and unreachable-state optimization may transform it. A default supplies RTL recovery; physical recovery requires checking the synthesized FSM.

options.text: `z` is a Moore output
options.explanation: True. It depends only on `state`, not on `x`, so it is Moore. Decoding state bits can glitch during transitions; the definition alone does not guarantee a glitch-free physical output.

options.text: The `case` statement is evaluated only at the rising edge of `clk`
options.explanation: False. `always @(*)` re-evaluates whenever any signal it reads (`state` or `x`) changes. It is combinational logic that is always computing; only the `state` register waits for the edge.

questions.workedExample:
Map the code to the FSM block diagram:

```
always @(posedge clk) -> state reg
always @(*) case      -> next-state
assign z              -> output
```

1. All three are concurrent hardware (A true).
2. Whether something becomes a flip-flop depends on *how* it is assigned (on a clock edge), not on the keyword `reg` (B false).
3. Every combinational output must be assigned on every path; `default` guarantees it (C true).
4. `z = (state == S2)` uses only state: Moore (D true).
5. The case block has no clock in its sensitivity list, so it responds to every change of `state` or `x` (E false).
